title: RSC vs Client Components — when do you add 'use client' in Next.js 15?
description: Explain the server/client component boundary, why it exists, and the rules for picking one in the App Router.
answer:
RSCs run only on the server, can be async and touch the DB with zero JS shipped; Client Components run on both.
Next.js 15 defaults every component in `app/` to a React Server Component. You add `'use client'` when a component needs anything that only the browser can do: `useState`, `useReducer`, `useEffect`, `useRef` with DOM mutation, event handlers, or Web APIs like `localStorage`. Props crossing the boundary must be serializable. You cannot pass functions that close over server state, Dates without care, or non-serializable classes. | Aspect | Server Component | Client Component (`'use client'`) | |---|---|---| | Where it runs | Server only | Server (SSR) + Client (hydrate) | | Can be `async` / access DB | Yes | No | **Interview Tip:** If asked to refactor a slow page, say: lift `fetch` into the RSC page, remove `useEffect` waterfalls. ```tsx // app/products/page.tsx — RSC (no 'use client') import { db } from '@/lib/db' import AddToCart from './AddToCart' // Client Component export default async function // trimmed ```

title: React Compiler — how does auto-memoization work in React 19?
description: Explain what the React Compiler does, why it removes manual memo, and its limits.
answer:
The React Compiler (formerly React Forget) is a Babel/SWC build-time transform that automatically memoizes computations.
Before the Compiler, you wrapped expensive calculations in `useMemo` and callbacks in `useCallback` with manual dependency arrays. Get a dep wrong and you either recompute too often or read stale values. Under the hood it treats components as pure functions of props and state. For performance, this is a step change. Shopify and Meta report 2–3× fewer re-renders without touching source. | Approach | How deps are tracked | Correctness risk | Bundle cost | |---|---|---|---| | Manual `useMemo` | You list deps | High (stale/missing deps) | None | | React Compiler | Compiler infers | Low (bails out if unsafe) | ~1–2 KB runtime | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I let the Compiler handle memoization and use `eslint-plugin-react-compiler` in CI. ```js // next.config.js — enable Compiler in Next.js 15 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ const nextConfig = { experimental: { reactCompiler: true }, } export default // trimmed ```

title: Server Actions — how do mutations work without API routes in Next.js 15?
description: Describe `'use server'`, action invocation from Client Components, and security/serialization rules.
answer:
Server Actions are async functions marked with `'use server'` that run on the server but are callable from Client Components or `

You define an action in a `app/actions.ts` file with `'use server'` at the top, or inline inside an RSC. The function can take `FormData` or serializable args, validate with Zod, touch the database, and call `revalidatePath()` or `revalidateTag()`. Security is explicit: actions run with server authority, so you must authorize by reading `cookies()`/`headers()` and checking the session inside the action, not trusting the client. In React 19, actions integrate with `useActionState` and `useFormStatus` for pending/error/optimistic handling as a transition. They also support `useOptimistic` for instant UI. | Approach | Endpoint | JS needed | Auth | Validation | |---|---|---|---|---| | API Route (`/api`) | Manual `route.ts` | Client fetch | Manual header check | Manual | | Server Action | Auto-generated | Optional (progressive) | `cookies()`/`auth()` | Zod on server | **Interview Tip:** Whiteboard the flow: Client → serialized action call → server executes with DB → `revalidatePath('/todos')` → updated RSC. ```tsx // app/actions.ts 'use server' import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache' export async function createTodo(formData: FormData) { const title = String(formData.get('title')) if (!title.trim()) return { // trimmed ```

title: useFormStatus & useActionState — modern form handling in React 19
description: Explain how `useFormStatus` and `useActionState` replace manual pending/error state for forms.
answer:
`useActionState` (replaces `useFormState`) wraps a Server Action and returns `[state, action, isPending]` — the current result, a dispatchable action, and pending flag.
Before React 19, form handling meant `useState` for pending, error, and result. `useActionState` collapses that: `const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(createTodo, {error: null})`. You pass `formAction` to `
`. `useFormStatus` solves the prop-drilling problem for pending UI. A `` rendered deep inside the form can call `const {pending, data, method} = useFormStatus()` and disable itself while the action runs, show a spinner, or read the submitted `FormData`. Interviewers expect you to contrast `useActionState` vs `useTransition`: `useActionState` is purpose-built for forms and holds the action's result state, while `useTransition` is generic. | Hook | Where used | What it returns | Use case | |---|---|---|---| | `useActionState` | Form parent | `[state, action, pending]` | Hold result/errors | | `useFormStatus` | Button/child | `{pending, data, action}` | Disable button, show spinner | **Interview Tip:** Mention the naming migration (`useFormState` → `useActionState`) and that `useFormStatus` must be in a child of the form. ```tsx 'use client' import { useActionState } from 'react' import { useFormStatus } from 'react-dom' import { createTodo } from './actions' function Submit() { const // trimmed ```

title: cache() and fetch memoization — request deduplication in RSC
answer:
`cache()` (from `react`) memoizes a function's result per server render — same args return the same Promise, so ten components calling `getUser(1)`.
In RSC, data fetching is just function calls: `await db.user.findUnique({where:{id}})` or `fetch(...)`. Without `cache()`, two components fetching the same user would hit the DB twice. Next.js 15's `fetch` adds a second layer: the Data Cache. `fetch('/api/user/1', {next:{revalidate: 60, tags:['user-1']}})` caches the result for 60s or until `revalidateTag('user-1')` is called from a Server Action. Uncached `fetch(...,{cache:'no-store'})` opts out. Common interview trap: waterfalls. If you `await` sequentially in one RSC (`const a=await getA(); const b=await getB()`), you serialize. | Layer | Scope | API | Invalidation | |---|---|---|---| | Request Memo | Single render | `cache()`, `fetch` dedupe | Auto (per request) | | Data Cache | Cross-request | `fetch` + `unstable_cache` | `revalidateTag`/`revalidatePath` | **Interview Tip:** Draw two layers on the whiteboard: per-render memo (dedup) vs cross-request Data Cache (revalidate). ```ts import { cache } from 'react' import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache' // Per-render dedupe — same Promise for same id in one request // trimmed ```

title: Error Boundaries with RSC — why can't Server Components catch errors?
description: Explain error boundary placement, RSC error bubbling, and Next.js error.tsx conventions.
answer:
React Server Components cannot be Error Boundaries themselves — boundaries must be Client Components (`'use client'`).
Error Boundaries are class components (or Next.js `error.tsx` files which are client boundaries under the hood) because they rely on lifecycle methods `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch` that only run on the client. In Next.js 15 this maps to file conventions: `error.tsx` next to a `page.tsx` catches errors for that segment, `global-error.tsx` catches root errors, and `not-found.tsx` handles 404s. Best practice: keep boundaries small and composable — wrap each data widget in its own `ErrorBoundary` so one failing widget doesn't take down the whole page. | Concept | Where it runs | Catches RSC errors | Fallback | |---|---|---|---| | `Suspense` | Client | No (only pending) | `fallback` prop | | `ErrorBoundary` (`'use client'`) | Client | Yes | `fallback` prop | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'Boundaries must be Client Components — I put a small boundary around each RSC widget, and use. ```tsx // app/dashboard/error.tsx — client boundary for RSC segment 'use client' export default function Error({ error, reset }: {error: Error, reset: ()=>void}) { return

title: Next.js instrumentation hook — observability in Next.js 15
description: Explain `instrumentation.ts`, when it runs, and what to do with OpenTelemetry, Sentry, etc.
answer:
Next.js 15's `instrumentation.ts` (or `instrumentation.js`) exports a `register()` function that runs once when the server starts (Node and Edge, if defined), before.
You enable it by creating `src/instrumentation.ts` and setting `experimental.instrumentationHook: true` in earlier versions; in Next.js 15 it is stable and on by default when the file exists. Typical setups: for OpenTelemetry, `import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel'` with `serviceName`; for Sentry, `Sentry.init({dsn, tracesSampleRate})`; for custom metrics, start a `pino` logger or `prom-client`. Pitfalls: it runs only on the server, not in the browser, and it runs in a bare context — don't access `cookies()` or DB there. Keep it lean; heavy imports delay server start. | Hook | When | Runtime | Use | |---|---|---|---| | `instrumentation.ts` `register()` | Once at boot | Node + Edge | OTEL/Sentry init | | `onRequestError` | On server error | Both | Central error logging | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I put OTEL setup in instrumentation.ts so all Server Actions and RSCs are traced automatically. ```ts // instrumentation.ts — Next.js 15 import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel' export async function register() { if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'nodejs') { await import('pino') registerOTel({ // trimmed ```

title: Async Server Components & waterfall prevention — fetching without blocking
description: Explain async RSC, parallel fetching with Promise.all, and hoisting promises.
answer:
Async Server Components can `await` directly, but `await`ing sequentially creates waterfalls.
A naive RSC does `const user = await getUser(); const posts = await getPosts(user.id)` — the second fetch can't start until the first finishes, so latency adds. For components that don't need each other's data, go further with render-as-you-fetch: in the parent RSC, do `const commentsPromise = fetchComments()` (no await) and pass `commentsPromise` to a child Client or Server Component that does `const comments =. Interviewers expect you to spot waterfalls in code review. When you see a client `useEffect` chain or sequential RSC awaits, suggest hoisting promises and adding `` per widget. | Pattern | Latency | Code shape | Streaming | |---|---|---|---| | Sequential `await` | a + b | `await a; await b` | Blocked | | `Promise.all` | max(a,b) | `Promise.all([aP,bP])` | Together | **Interview Tip:** When you see `await` inside a loop or sequential awaits, say: 'Hoist promises and Promise.all. ```tsx // app/page.tsx — RSC, parallel fetching import { Suspense } from 'react' async function Comments({ promise }) { const c = await promise; return // trimmed ```

The Compiler is conservative for correctness. If you write `function Card({item}) { item.count++ ; return ... title: Partial Prerendering (PPR) in Next.js 15 — static shell + dynamic holes
description: Explain PPR, how it combines static and dynamic rendering with Suspense holes.
answer:
Partial Prerendering (Next.js 15 stable) prerenders the static parts of a route at build time and leaves dynamic parts as Suspense holes that render on each.
Before PPR, a route was either fully static (no `cookies()`/`fetch` with `no-store`) or fully dynamic (any dynamic API made the whole page dynamic). That meant a single personalized widget forced the entire page to render per request. Implementation is declarative: keep the page as an RSC, extract the user-specific part like `}>` where `UserGreeting` is `async` and reads `cookies()`. Next.js static analysis detects the dynamic boundary and splits the build output. For interviews, contrast PPR with ISR and Streaming: ISR revalidates the whole page after N seconds; PPR keeps the static shell forever cached at the edge and only re-renders the holes per request; Streaming SSR streams without prerendering. | Rendering | Shell | Dynamic part | TTFB | |---|---|---|---| | Fully static | Build-time | None | Fast (CDN) | | Fully dynamic | Per-request | Whole page | Slower | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I enable PPR and isolate cookies()/auth to a small Suspense boundary — the rest stays static and cached at the edge,. ```tsx // next.config.js — enable PPR in Next 15 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ const nextConfig = { experimental: { ppr: 'incremental' } } export default nextConfig // app/page.tsx — PPR with Suspense hole // ... trimmed for brevity ```
